title: Quadratics, parabolas and higher powers
hook: A 12 V battery with 0.5 Ω inside it feeds a load. What current gives the load the most power, and why is it exactly half the short-circuit current?
oneBreath: A quadratic is a rule whose highest power is x², and you can write the same one three ways: spread out, as a square plus a number, or, when it has them, as two brackets multiplied. The brackets show where its U-shaped graph crosses the axis, the square shows where it turns, and one formula finds the answers when neither comes easily. The same shape gives a thrown ball's highest point and the load that draws most power from a supply, and a rule with higher powers, such as x³, has a bracket (x − a) for every number a that makes it zero.

ideas.title: Two brackets as an area
ideas.oneLine: Two brackets multiply as the four tiles of a rectangle with those sides: (x + 3)(x + 2) = x² + 5x + 6.

ideas.title: Factorising quadratics
ideas.oneLine: Factorising undoes expanding: two numbers multiplying to 6 and adding to 5 split x² + 5x + 6 into (x + 2)(x + 3).

ideas.title: Solving by factorising
ideas.oneLine: A product is zero only if a factor is zero, so (x − 2)(x − 5) = 0 gives x = 2 or 5.

ideas.title: Completing the square
ideas.oneLine: Add the missing corner and x² + 6x + 2 becomes (x + 3)² − 7, a form that shows its lowest value at once.

ideas.title: The quadratic formula
ideas.oneLine: Completing the square with letters gives x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) ÷ 2a, the answers to any quadratic equation that has them.

ideas.title: The parabola from its rule
ideas.oneLine: Three clues in the rule sketch a quadratic's U-shaped graph: a's sign gives which way up, c the y-crossing, the roots the x-crossings.

ideas.title: Quadratics at work
ideas.oneLine: A thrown ball's height, a load's power against current and a loaded beam's bending rise and fall as quadratics, peaking halfway between two zeros.

ideas.title: Higher powers
ideas.oneLine: If putting x = a into a polynomial, a sum of whole-number powers of x, gives 0, then (x − a) is one of its factors.

calibration.q: A square patio is x metres along each side. You make each side 2 metres longer. How much more area does it have, in square metres?
calibration.why: The new patio is (x + 2)², which is x² + 4x + 4: two strips of 2 by x and a 2 by 2 corner. Adding 4 alone squares each part and forgets both strips, and 2x + 4 counts only one strip.

calibration.q: Which values of x make x² = 6x true?
calibration.why: Try 0: 0² is 0 and 6 × 0 is 0, so it works, and 6 works too, since 36 = 36. Dividing both sides by x gives only 6, because it quietly throws away x = 0.
